Fixture: The Cost Still to Pay

A short source document in the house format, for the tests (a test fixture, not a real explainer)
November 2026
Abstract. A test fixture, not a real explainer: a short source document in the house format that the tests plan video series from. A receding-window controller pays a boundary term $W$ at the end of its window. When $W$ falls at least as fast as cost is spent, the least cost still to pay falls at every step (Keerthi & Gilbert, 1988; Mayne et al., 2000). On a ball balanced on a hilltop, that cost still to pay generates the momentum, solves the Hamilton–Jacobi equation at zero energy, and certifies every boundary term with $H(q,-\nabla W)\ge 0$. Every number is printed by a script in code/.

1. The Idea in One Picture

A predictive controller looks ahead over a window of $N$ steps, chooses the cheapest way through it, applies the first step and starts again from where it lands. What it plans is a trade: the cost of the steps inside the window against a price $W$ for the state where the window ends. This document follows one question through that trade: when does the price at the end make the whole loop settle?

1.1 A window and a boundary term

The least cost of a window that starts at $q$ is the value

$$ V_N(q)=\min_{q_1,\dots,q_N}\;\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}L_d(q_k,q_{k+1})+W(q_N),\qquad q_0=q. \tag{1} $$

Here $L_d(q_k,q_{k+1})$ is the cost of one step and $W$ the boundary term. The controller applies the first step of the minimizer and solves the same problem again at the next state. Nothing in the definition says that $V_N$ falls along the closed loop: that depends on the pair of cost and boundary term, and the next section names the condition.

The picture to keep is a ball on a hill. Pushing costs effort, standing away from the summit costs too, and the window plans a few pushes ahead. The boundary term says what it costs to be left at the end of the window, and everything below asks whether that statement is honest.

2. The Remaining Action

Call $V_N$ in (1) the remaining action: the cost still to pay from here on, as far as the window can see. The classical argument of receding-window control compares the window from $q$ with the window one step later.

2.1 The local rule

Suppose there is a step $\varphi(q)$ near the target along which the boundary term falls at least as fast as cost is spent:

$$ W\big(\varphi(q)\big)-W(q)\le -L_d\big(q,\varphi(q)\big). \tag{2} $$

Then the tail of yesterday's plan, extended by one such step, is an admissible plan for today, and the value falls by at least the cost of the step that was applied:

$$ V_N(q^+)-V_N(q)\le -L_d(q,q^+). \tag{3} $$

The rule is local: it asks one inequality of $W$ near the target, and the descent (3) holds for every window length $N$.

2.2 When the boundary term is exact

If $W$ is the true infinite-horizon value and the step cost is computed exactly along the optimal motion, the inequality (2) holds with equality, and so does the descent. On the hilltop of the next section, with a step of $h=0.1$, one step shrinks the state by the factor $0.904837$, the value falls from $0.5$ to $0.409365$ and the step costs $0.090635$: the descent defect is zero to rounding. Any other pair leaves a gap, and the gap is the price of an inexact boundary term.

3. The Hilltop: Hamilton–Jacobi and the Stable Manifold

Shrink the step to zero and the window problem becomes a problem in continuous time. Take a ball of mass $m$ on an inverted parabola and charge it for speed and for distance from the summit:

$$ L(q,v)=\tfrac12 m v^2+\tfrac12\kappa q^2 . \tag{4} $$

Read as kinetic minus potential energy, the potential is $-\tfrac12\kappa q^2$: a hilltop. Its Euler–Lagrange equation $m\ddot q=\kappa q$ has the solutions $e^{\pm\omega t}$ with $\omega=\sqrt{\kappa/m}$, and only the decaying one arrives at the summit and stops there.

3.1 The momentum is a gradient

Along the arriving motion $q(t)=q_0e^{-\omega t}$ the cost still to pay is

$$ V(q)=\tfrac12\sqrt{m\kappa}\,q^2,\qquad p=-V'(q). \tag{5} $$

With $m=\kappa=1$ and $q_0=1$: $\omega=1$, $V(1)=0.5$, and the integral of $L$ along the motion is $0.5$ as well. The momentum of the arriving motion is minus the gradient of the cost still to pay.

3.2 The certificate

The Hamiltonian of (4) is

$$ H(q,p)=\frac{p^2}{2m}-\tfrac12\kappa q^2 , \tag{6} $$

and $V$ solves the Hamilton–Jacobi equation at zero energy, $H(q,-V'(q))=0$. Shrinking the window turns the local rule (2) into a condition on any boundary term $W$:

$$ H\big(q,-\nabla W(q)\big)\ge 0 . \tag{7} $$

3.3 Scaled candidates

For $W=cV$ the left side of (7) is $\tfrac12\kappa q^2(c^2-1)$. At $\kappa=q=1$:

$c$$H(q,-cV')$
$0.5$−0.375
$1$0
$2$1.5

Every $c\ge1$ is certified; $c=1$ is the exact boundary term, where the window value of (1) no longer depends on $N$.

4. A Speed Limit

Now cap the speed: $|v|\le\bar v$. Far from the summit the free motion would be faster than allowed, so the best law moves at the limit until the state reaches $q_s=\bar v/\omega$, and from there follows the free motion of (5). With $m=\kappa=1$, $\bar v=0.4$ and $q_0=1$ the switch is at $q_s=0.4$ and the clipped law costs $0.59$, which is $0.09$ more than the unconstrained $V(1)=0.5$.

The certificate (7) still decides which boundary terms are honest, with the Hamiltonian of the constrained problem in place of (6). The window of (1) does not change: only the set of admissible steps does.

The speed limit shows the general pattern. A constraint changes the cost still to pay, and with it the exact boundary term; a boundary term that was exact without the constraint can stop being certified with it.
